1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6.name: Pirc Defence
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6.strategy: The defining move of the Pirc: Black prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and press on the centre from a distance instead of occupying it. White is invited to build a big pawn centre, and Black bets on undermining it later with the bishop and with pawn breaks on the flanks.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nbd7.name: Lion Defence
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nbd7.background: In recent years Black has tried this move order starting with 1...d6 to reach the improved Hanham set-up of the Philidor Defence while avoiding White's early dxe5 and Bc4 options.
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nbd7.strategy: Prepares ...e5 with the knight already in place, so that the d-file stays closed to White's queen and Black can recapture on e5 with a piece instead of trading queens and losing the right to castle. The knight blocks the c8 bishop for now, and White may choose a sharper set-up than simple development.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5.strategy: Contests the centre with a pawn at once, aiming at a solid pair of pawns on d6 and e5 behind which the pieces develop. If White develops, the game is calm; but White can also exchange pawns and queens, leaving Black unable to castle in a slightly worse endgame.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 c6.name: Czech Defence
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 c6.background: It has also been called the Pribyl System.
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 c6.strategy: A flexible sideline: the pawn opens a diagonal for the queen and prepares expansion on the queenside, while Black keeps a fianchetto and a central break both in reserve. It costs time in the fight for the centre, which White can use to build a broad pawn centre.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops and attacks the e5 pawn a second time, so Black must support it at once. It leads to a calm game with a small space edge for White. Trading pawns and queens first is the other way to play, and gives White only a small endgame edge.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5 4.dxe5.strategy: Settles the centre at once: after ...dxe5 White can trade queens, which costs Black the right to castle, and keeps a small, safe edge in a calm endgame. Black's position is solid, so the edge is hard to enlarge and the game is a patient one.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nge2.strategy: Supports d4 and the knight on c3 without blocking the f-pawn, a flexible way to keep the central tension. The knight shuts in the king's bishop, though, so White develops more slowly and the edge, if any, is small.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7.name: Philidor Defence: Lion Variation
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7.background: Tony Kosten called this move order the "improved" Hanham Variation; the original is named after the American master James Moore Hanham.
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7.strategy: Adds a defender to the pawn that is attacked twice, and avoids ...Nc6, where Bb5 would pin the knight. Black keeps the centre solid and keeps castling, though the knight blocks the c8 bishop and the position stays a little passive for now.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 exd4.strategy: Trades the e-pawn for White's d-pawn and opens the game. Black has no pawn to defend and the pieces get free lines, but the recapturing knight lands in the centre and White keeps more space, so Black plays for equality rather than the initiative.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Defends e5 and eyes d4 with a developing move, but the knight can be pinned to the king by Bb5 and driven back by d5 with a gain of space. Black loses time sorting this out and ends up passive.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7 5.B.strategy: Trains the bishop on f7, which only the king guards, and prepares castling. It asks Black to find a safe set-up without weakening e5, and keeps the centre tense: White plays for a slow squeeze rather than an immediate break.
The modest developing move: the bishop heads for castling and stays flexible, but gives up the pressure on f7. White plays for a slow game in the centre, and Black's solid set-up is hard to dislodge.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7 5.g.name: Philidor Defence: Lion Variation, Shirov Gambit
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7 5.g.strategy: A gambit: the g-pawn is offered because the knight on f6 can take it, and White hopes for the half-open g-file and the threat of pushing on to cramp the knight. If Black takes and defends carefully, White has to prove that the attack is worth the pawn and the loosened kingside.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7 5.B.strategy: Develops the bishop and clears the way for castling, after which the rook guards f7 against the bishop on c4. The pawns on d6 and e5 stay where they are, so the central tension remains and Black waits for White to commit.

Gives up the strongpoint on e5 that the set-up was built around and opens the game for a plain exchange structure, a pawn on d6 against White's on e4. With the bishop on c4 aiming at f7 Black has to castle soon, while White's pieces take the central squares.

Takes g5 from the knight and the bishop in advance, so neither Ng5 against f7 nor Bg5 against the knight on f6 is possible. The price is a tempo and a pawn move on the kingside before Black has castled, which gives White time to castle and build up pressure in the centre.

Brings the king to safety before anything else and keeps the tension in the centre intact. Black must now finish development and find counterplay, while White keeps the choice between a central break and a slow build-up.
Resolves the central tension too early: Black recaptures with pawn or knight and finishes development without difficulty, and White has nothing concrete to show for the opened centre.

Doubles the attack on f7 and, once Black castles, threatens a sacrifice there followed by a knight raid that wins material. But the knight ends up stranded on the rim while Black gets a strong initiative for the material, so the plan backfires and White loses time.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7 5.B.name: Philidor Defence: Lion Variation, Bishop Sacrifice
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7 5.B.strategy: A speculative sacrifice: the bishop goes for a pawn in the hope of dragging the king into the open for tricks with the knight. Black just takes it, and White has a piece less for a pawn and no attack to show for it.

Recaptures with the pawn rather than the knight, keeping a pawn on e5 with the d7-knight as its defender, and opens the d-file. Black gets a solid structure but a slightly passive one, with the knight tied to the defence of e5.

Black recaptures with a knight and heads for simplification. If the knights and queens come off, Black keeps the right to castle and a sound pawn on e5, but the bishop on c4 stays the more active piece and the game offers Black little to play for.
Counterattacks on e5 and f2 instead of recapturing, but 7.exd6 Bxd6 leaves Black a pawn down, with the knight offside and no real threat.

Castles and lets White go for the sacrifice on f7: White ends up ahead on material, but the knight is stranded on the edge of the board and Black gets a strong initiative. That makes 6.Ng5 the inferior try.
Kicks the knight but ignores f7: Nxf7 forks queen and rook, and the king cannot take because the bishop on c4 guards the square. Black loses at least the exchange and a pawn.
Hits the bishop but leaves f7 to its fate: Bxf7+ wins a pawn, since the king cannot take with the knight on g5 guarding the square, and Black loses the right to castle.
Castles at once: the king is safe, the rook now guards f7, and the pressure from the bishop on c4 loses its sting. Black keeps the centre pawns where they are and plays for a patient, solid game.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7 5.B.name: Philidor Defence: Lion Variation, Lion's Claw, with Bc4 and h6
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7 5.B.strategy: Takes g5 from White's knight and bishop before they can use it, so the pressure on f7 loses its sting, at the cost of a tempo and a pawn move on the kingside that is not needed yet. Black leaves the king in the centre a little longer and plays a patient game.

Releases the tension and heads for a plain structure with a pawn on d6 against White's on e4. Black gives up the strongpoint on e5 and the compact set-up around it, so White's knight and bishop take active posts and Black has a solid but slightly cramped game.

Develops the bishop behind the pawn chain, where it protects the centre rather than aiming at anything, and prepares castling. Black builds a compact, patient defence of e5 and holds the central tension instead of releasing it.
Takes b5 and d5 from White's pieces and frees c7 for the queen, so Black can build the compact set-up around e5 in either order. The cost is some space and a move that develops no piece.

Releases the central tension at once: the pieces get open lines and Black has no pawn on e5 to look after. In return the strongpoint the set-up was built around is gone, and White's recapturing piece settles in the centre with a small space edge.

Castles before committing the centre, so White can meet whatever Black chooses. The position has no quick break against Black's solid set-up, and the game becomes a manoeuvring fight over the tension on d4 and e5: space against solidity.

Closes the centre and wins space, fixing a pawn chain that leaves e5 solidly defended. The price is the tension: White no longer cramps Black, whose pieces find good squares and whose play shifts to the wings, so the space edge is safe but hard to use.
Resolves the tension: after ...dxe5 the pawn structure is symmetrical and White's central space edge is gone. The game is level and turns on piece placement rather than on any pawn break.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7 5.B.name: Philidor Defence: Lion Variation, Lion's Claw, with Be2 and c6
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7 5.B.strategy: Completes a compact set-up around e5: pawn on d6, knights on d7 and f6, bishop on e7. The pawn on c6 takes b5 and d5 away from White's pieces, so Black keeps a firm grip on e5 and can wait, at the cost of space.

Puts the king on the safe side first and keeps the choice of pawn moves open. Black reaches the same compact set-up around e5 by a different route; the pawn on c6 is only needed later, once White shows a plan.
Resolves the centre with the king still uncastled: White recaptures in the centre and Black castles next. Black gets a free, equal game, but the compact set-up around e5 is gone for good.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Nf3.name: Pirc Defence: Classical Variation
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Nf3.background: Also known as the Two Knights System. Efim Geller, Anatoly Karpov and Evgeni Vasiukov have all used it successfully with White, and Zurab Azmaiparashvili has scored well against it with Black.
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Nf3.strategy: The classical move: develops the king's knight and covers d4 and e5 while the pawns on e4 and d4 stay unpushed. White gets central space with a solid structure and castles quickly, while Black's counterplay depends on hitting the centre at the right moment.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4.name: Pirc Defence: Austrian Attack
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4.background: Siegbert Tarrasch used it to beat Rudolf Charousek in 17 moves in 1896. In the 1972 World Championship game against Fischer's Pirc, Boris Spassky played it.
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4.strategy: Builds a broad centre of e4, d4 and f4 and prepares the push e5 to cramp Black and support a kingside attack. The cost is a loosened kingside, and Black must strike at the centre in time with a pawn break or be squeezed.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be3.strategy: Flexible development with an eye on the queen coming to d2 and castling long, after which White can storm the kingside, or on a quieter set-up. The bishop backs up d4 and commits neither the f-pawn nor the king's knight yet.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be2.strategy: Modest, flexible development: the bishop prepares castling and White decides later between a classical set-up and an aggressive attack on the wing. Black gets time to complete the fianchetto, so White needs a plan quickly.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Bg5.name: Pirc Defence: Byrne Variation
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Bg5.background: Robert Byrne introduced it in the 1960s.
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Bg5.strategy: Hits the knight that attacks e4 and prepares to bring the queen to d2 and the bishop to h6 against Black's fianchettoed bishop. Sound, and it can set a small trap, but Black can delay the fianchetto and keep the position flexible.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.g3.name: Pirc Defence: Sveshnikov System
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.g3.strategy: A quiet fianchetto for White: the bishop on g2 will support e4 along the long diagonal, and the f-pawn can stay at home. Solid but slow, it gives up the aggressive set-ups and gives Black time to complete the plan.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Bc4.name: Pirc Defence: Kholmov System
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Bc4.strategy: Aims the bishop at f7 before the knight comes out, an off-beat try for the initiative rather than a recommended line. The bishop can lose time when Black strikes in the centre with tempo, and Black has sound ways to equalise.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be2 Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop now stands on the long diagonal against the centre, and Black can castle. This is the whole point of the opening, a flexible, solid set-up that waits for White to overextend.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be2 c6.strategy: Keeps the structure flexible: the pawn takes d5 and b5 from White's pieces and prepares queenside play while the fianchetto waits. It costs time, and with the bishop still on f8 White gets a free hand to build in the centre.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be2 Nbd7.strategy: Heads for a central break with the e-pawn, the knight supporting it from d7, and keeps the fianchetto available. The cost is a passive set-up: the knight blocks the bishop on c8, and White's centre gets time to expand before Black has finished developing.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be2 Bg7 5.h4.name: Pirc Defence: Bayonet Attack
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be2 Bg7 5.h4.strategy: Advances the h-pawn to pry open the h-file with h5 and aim at the kingside. It gains space on the wing, but it weakens White's own king and commits to an attack before Black's centre has been challenged.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be2 Bg7 5.g4.name: Pirc Defence: Chinese Variation
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be2 Bg7 5.g4.strategy: Gains space with the g-pawn and threatens to chase the f6 knight with g5, an aggressive but very committal plan. The pawn is protected by the bishop, with the queen behind it, but it loosens White's kingside and Black can counter in the centre.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be2 Bg7 5.Nf.strategy: Develops the kingside and heads for the classical set-up: White castles behind a broad, well-guarded pawn centre and does not commit to an early attack. A quiet manoeuvring game follows in which White's extra space is real but gives Black targets for timely central breaks.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be3 c6.strategy: Prepares queenside counterplay with the c-pawn and the queen, and keeps the fianchetto in reserve until White shows a plan. The play is aimed at the queenside, where White may castle.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be3 Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto at once and puts the bishop on the long diagonal against White's centre. White's plan of Qd2 and Bh6 to trade it is the point to watch: Black has to meet the kingside pressure with quick counterplay in the centre or on the queenside.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be3 Bg4.strategy: Hits the queen at once and puts the bishop outside the pawn chain, but White gains time by challenging it, and the knight on f6 already guards g4 so the queen cannot take it. The bishop gets no lasting target and Black's development stays behind.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be3 c6 5.Qd2.name: Pirc Defence: 150 Attack
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be3 c6 5.Qd2.background: British players such as Mark Hebden, Paul Motwani, Gary Lane and later Michael Adams played Be3 and Qd2 without f3 and called it the 150 Attack, because players of that strength (150 ECF, about 1825 Elo) can play the position well without theory.
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be3 c6 5.Qd2.strategy: Backs up the bishop on e3 and prepares to castle long and storm the kingside, with Bh6 to trade off Black's fianchettoed bishop. It needs little theory, but it commits the king to the queenside, just where Black's counterplay is aimed.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be3 c6 5.h3.name: Pirc Defence: 150 Attack, Sveshnikov-Jansa Attack
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be3 c6 5.h3.strategy: A flexible waiting move: it takes g4 from the black bishop and keeps White's options open between expanding on the kingside and a quieter set-up. It is slower than the queen move and gives Black time to organise counterplay on the queenside.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be3 c6 5.f3.strategy: Props up e4 and takes g4 from Black's pieces, a solid base for Qd2, long castling and a kingside pawn storm. It commits White to that plan and takes f3 from the knight, so the game becomes a race between White's kingside attack and Black's queenside play.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be3 c6 5.Qd2.name: Pirc Defence: 150 Attack, Inner Doll Defence
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be3 c6 5.Qd2.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before it gets locked in and discourages the king's knight: Nf3 would allow a trade that doubles White's pawns. White can simply chase the bishop away, so Black spends time before getting any active play.

Meets White's long-castling plan head-on: the pawn gains queenside space and prepares to harass the knight on c3 and to develop the bishop on b7. It loosens Black's own queenside, and the dark-squared bishop is still waiting, so the Bh6 idea must be watched.

Completes the fianchetto and fights the centre from a distance. It invites Bh6: the trade takes away Black's main piece and leaves White's queen in charge of the dark squares around the king, so Black has to find counterplay fast.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto at once: the bishop stands ready on the long diagonal, behind the f6 knight, to press on d4 and e5 once the knight moves. Black can castle next and wait for the right moment to strike at the centre.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 before White has developed and challenges the centre at once. The cost is time: with the bishop still on f8, the recapture ...dxc5 allows an early queen trade that costs Black the right to castle, so Black risks falling behind.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 Nc6.strategy: Develops the queenside knight and adds to the pressure on d4, but it blocks the c-pawn and meets d5 at once, when the pawn on f4 takes e5 away and the knight is left with only poor squares. White gains space and time.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 Bg7 5.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight and guards e5 and d4, so the central advance becomes a real threat. Black must be prompt about counterplay, by castling and striking at the centre, or White's space will tell.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 Bg7 5.Bc4.name: Pirc Defence: Austrian Attack, Ljubojevic Variation
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 Bg7 5.Bc4.strategy: Puts the bishop on the a2-g8 diagonal before developing the knight, aiming at f7. It asks little of Black, who can develop calmly and challenge the centre with tempo, so White gets complications rather than an advantage.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 Bg7 5.Bd3.strategy: Develops the bishop where it backs e4 and leaves f3 free for the knight. White keeps the central pawns intact but delays the knight, which gives Black time to organise a counter-strike at the centre.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 Bg7 5.Nf3.name: Pirc Defence: Austrian Attack
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 Bg7 5.Nf3.strategy: Gets the king to safety before White's centre advances. Black prepares to strike at that centre with a pawn break and to counterattack.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 Bg7 5.Nf3.name: Pirc Defence: Austrian Attack, Dragon Formation
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 Bg7 5.Nf3.strategy: Strikes at the d4 pawn at once instead of castling, accepting the risk of White's central push and checks in exchange for early counterplay on the queenside. It is sharper than castling and demands accurate play from both sides.

Adds the queenside knight's pressure on d4 to the bishop's, but it blocks the c-pawn and meets tempo gains: Bb5 pins the knight to the king and d5 drives it back with a gain of space. Black risks falling behind in development.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 Bg7 5.Nf3.name: Pirc Defence: Austrian Attack, Weiss Variation
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 Bg7 5.Nf3.background: It is the most frequently played move here. White players, Fischer among them, turned to it after Fischer lost with 6.Be2 to Viktor Korchnoi at Curaçao in 1962.
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 Bg7 5.Nf3.strategy: Develops the bishop to a square where it defends e4 and prepares castling, keeping the push e5 in reserve. It is the main continuation: solid, flexible, and Black has to find counterplay against a big centre.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 Bg7 5.Nf3.name: Pirc Defence: Austrian Attack, Kurajica Variation
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 Bg7 5.Nf3.background: First extensively explored in the 1970s and played by Bojan Kurajica, Yuri Balashov and Alexander Beliavsky.
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 Bg7 5.Nf3.strategy: Develops the bishop to a square where it backs up the d4 pawn that Black's ...c5 and ...Nc6 attack, and leaves White the choice between pushing in the centre and a quieter set-up. It leads to sharp play.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 Bg7 5.Nf3.name: Pirc Defence: Austrian Attack, Unzicker Attack
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 Bg7 5.Nf3.background: Much played in the 1960s, though it has never become popular at the highest levels.
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 Bg7 5.Nf3.strategy: Strikes at once and drives the knight from f6, gaining space before Black is ready. But the advanced pawn can become a target and the consequences are unclear, which is why it never became a main line.

Challenges the head of White's chain at once: the retreat brings the knight and the bishop on the long diagonal into play against e5, which is now attacked three times, by the d6 pawn, the knight and the bishop. White's space edge is real, but the centre needs accurate defending.

Challenges the head of the chain by capturing, but after fxe5 the knight is attacked again and still has to move. White gets the pawn on e5 as a wedge that cramps Black, who has given up the d6 pawn that bore on it.
Retreats the knight while keeping the bishop and the d6 pawn aimed at e5. The knight is offside on e8 and blocks the rook, so White keeps the space edge and can build in comfort.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7.name: Pirc Defence: Classical Variation
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop on g7 lets Black castle and stands against the centre. Black answers the classical set-up with a compact, flexible structure and waits for a chance to break.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Nf3 c6.strategy: Keeps the fianchetto and a central break in reserve, takes d5 and b5 from White's pieces and gives the queen the c7 square. It delays Black's development, and White is free to expand in the centre before the bishop reaches g7.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Nf3 Nbd7.strategy: Prepares a central pawn break, the knight backing it from d7, while the bishop can still go to g7. It blocks the bishop on c8 and leaves White free to claim space, so Black's set-up is a little passive and waits for White to commit.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7 5.Be.name: Pirc Defence: Classical Variation, Quiet System
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7 5.Be.strategy: The classical set-up: the bishop prepares castling in a quiet, solid development with the centre pawns on e4 and d4. White's edge is space; Black gets time to castle and prepare a central break.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7 5.h3.name: Pirc Defence: Classical Variation, Schlechter Variation
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7 5.h3.strategy: Takes g4 from Black's c8 bishop, so the knight on f3 cannot be pinned against the queen. A useful waiting move, but it does little for development, so Black can castle and strike at the centre.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7 5.Bg.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and eyes the f6-knight, which guards e4. The pressure is slight: Black simply castles, and ...h6 asks the bishop to commit or retreat, so White has gained little for leaving the quiet set-up.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7 5.Be.strategy: Castles into safety and gets ready for a strike at the centre. Both sides have developed naturally and the game stays flexible, with Black's compact structure and White's extra space as the long-term trade.

A flexible, solid move: it takes b5 and d5 away from White's pieces and keeps the choice between a central break and queenside expansion open. It does not yet challenge the centre, so White can castle and build up without hindrance.

Develops with pressure on d4 and prepares to challenge the centre with a pawn. White can gain space with d5, which drives the knight away from the centre, so Black must be ready for a more closed game.

Completes kingside development and puts the king to safety while both centre pawns stay where they are. White forgoes the committal advance of the f-pawn and builds a compact, flexible centre, leaving Black to find where the counterplay will come from.

Develops the bishop to the square from which it guards d4, and keeps both ways of castling open. Black can harass the bishop with ...Ng4, but it has squares to go to, and White keeps a compact centre and a flexible plan.

Takes g4 away from Black's c8-bishop and the f6-knight, so the f3-knight cannot be pressed from there. It is a useful precaution but a slow one: White castles later, and Black gains a tempo to prepare a strike at the centre.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7 5.Be.name: Pirc Defence: Classical Variation, Quiet System, Chigorin Line
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7 5.Be.strategy: Develops with direct pressure on d4 and prepares to challenge the centre with a pawn. The price is that White can gain space by pushing d5 and forcing the knight to move, so Black must be ready for a more closed game.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7 5.Be.name: Pirc Defence: Classical Variation, Quiet System, Czech Defence
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7 5.Be.strategy: A solid, flexible move: it takes b5 and d5 away from White's pieces and prepares either a challenge to the centre or expansion on the queenside. It leaves the b8-knight without its most natural square, and Black keeps the plan open.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7 5.Be.name: Pirc Defence: Classical Variation, Quiet System, Parma Defence
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7 5.Be.strategy: Develops the light-squared bishop actively, outside the pawn chain, and pressures the f3-knight that guards d4 and e5. The cost is that taking on f3 gives White the bishop pair; Black accepts that to keep the fight for the centre going.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.f4.name: Lion Defence: Anti-Philidor
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.f4.strategy: The most ambitious reply: a third pawn in the centre strengthens control of e5, so Black's planned ...e5 meets real resistance, and White claims a broad centre with kingside space. It costs some solidity and commits White to a sharp fight over the centre.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.Nf3.strategy: The natural developing move: it guards d4 and e5 but does not stop Black from building the pawn structure it wants. White gets an easy, healthy game with a small space edge, but a less critical one than the sharper alternatives.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.g4.name: Lion Defence: Bayonet Attack
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.g4.strategy: A sharp flank thrust that threatens to gain space with g5 and drive the f6-knight from its good square. But it loosens White's own kingside before the pieces are out, and Black can strike at the centre at once: playable and risky, not best.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.f4 e5.name: Lion Defence: Anti-Philidor, Lion's Cave
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.f4 e5.strategy: Challenges the centre at once, hitting both d4 and f4. The d7-knight backs the pawn, so Black can meet the tension calmly; the cost is that e5 now comes under heavy pressure and the resulting fight has to be handled accurately.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.f4 g6.strategy: Heads for a Pirc-style fianchetto, but the knight on d7 already shuts in the c8-bishop, and White can push e5 at once, gaining space with tempo against the f6-knight. Sound, but Black is more cramped than the usual Pirc.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.f4 e6.strategy: A solid set-up that holds d5 and leaves the d6-pawn as the base of Black's structure. It is passive: the c8-bishop is hemmed in behind its own pawns, White enjoys a broad centre, and Black must find counterplay on the flanks later.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.f4 e5 5.Nf.strategy: Adds a third attacker to e5, which has only two defenders, so Black cannot simply hold it and the central tension must be resolved at once. White keeps the pawn centre intact for now and develops a piece with gain of time.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.f4 e5 5.dx.strategy: Opens the centre and trades off the d-pawn that anchors White's pawn centre. After the recapture the e5-pawn attacks f4, so White must recapture again to keep the pawn, and Black's pieces are comfortable: White gains little for releasing the tension.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.f4 e5 5.fx.strategy: Gives up the f4-pawn, the point of White's set-up, to open the f-file and the centre. After the exchanges the pawn centre is gone and the game is level, with Black's pieces at ease and White's king still in the middle.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.f4 e5 5.Nf.strategy: The way to resolve the tension: Black takes first, because waiting loses a pawn once White captures on e5 (a developing move such as ...Be7 fails to fxe5). Black gives up the e-pawn's central role but dissolves White's broad centre.

Takes the f-pawn instead of the d-pawn, which lets White recapture with a developing move and keep both centre pawns. Black has swapped off the wrong pawn: White develops with a free hand and Black has nothing to show for it.
Develops but ignores the tension in the centre: White takes on e5 and, once the pawns have been exchanged there, is a clean pawn up. Black needed to resolve the tension first.

Recaptures with the queen, which is centralised and hits the f6-knight and the d6 and a7 pawns at once. White keeps the lead in development and space; the queen can be harassed, but it has safe squares, so White keeps a small initiative.

Recaptures with a piece, so the queen stays at home out of reach of harassment. The knight is strong on d4, though ...c5 can ask it to move; White keeps the space and the lead in development and plays for a small edge.
Hangs the knight: the pawn on d4 attacks the c3-knight, so ...dxc3 wins a knight for a pawn, and the developing bishop move gives nothing back. White must recapture on d4 first.

Takes b5 and d5 away from White's pieces: no bishop pinning the d7-knight, no knight jumping to b5 to hit d6. It takes the sting out of White's active pieces and lets Black finish development quietly, though White keeps a small initiative.
Hits the queen with tempo and takes the d4 square, but at a structural price: d5 becomes a hole and the d6-pawn a target on the half-open d-file, which White's pieces can aim at.
Develops the bishop and prepares to castle, but leaves the queenside as it is: White's knight can jump to b5, hitting a7 twice and d6 at the same time, so Black must spend time answering it.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.Nf3 e5.strategy: Takes the central space Black has been waiting for. The d7-knight and d6 pawn support e5, and Black is content to see the centre opened by an exchange on e5. The structure is compact and sound, with a little less space than White.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.Nf3 c6.strategy: A flexible, solid move that takes b5 and d5 away from White's pieces and prepares either a central or a queenside plan. It claims no space yet, so White keeps the freer game and can build up the centre.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nbd7 4.Nf3 g6.strategy: Aims for the Pirc fianchetto, but with the knight already on d7 the c8-bishop is shut in and the usual plan is harder to carry out. White can challenge at once with e5, and Black has to calculate the exchanges that follow.
